'''Robert Judson Aley''' (May 11, 1863 – July 1, 1935) was an American mathematician, academic administrator, teacher and university president. Aley served as the fifth [[Presidents of the University of Maine|President]] of the [[University of Maine]] from January 1911 to August 1921, and then as President of [[Butler University|Butler College]] in Indianapolis, Indiana from 1921 to 1931.<ref name="Boop">{{cite book |last1=Boop |first1=Roger W. |title=Fulfilling the Charter: The Story of the College of Education at Butler University and More ... |date=2008 |publisher=iUniverse |isbn=978-0-595-44587-5 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jXkU9mic3H8C&q=%22Robert+Judson+Aley%22+Butler&pg=PA31 |language=en}}</ref>

==Education and early career==
Robert Judson Aley was born on May 11, 1863, in [[Coal City, Indiana]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fA8Ucif604oC |title=Old Penn: Weekly Magazine of the University of Pennsylvania |date=1916 |publisher=University of Pennsylvania. |pages=750 |language=en |via=[[Google Books]]}}</ref> He attended public schools.

Aley began his teaching career at the age of 14. After three years of teaching in rural schools, he attended and eventually graduated from [[Valparaiso University]] ([[Bachelor of Science]], 1882). He worked as a Principal in [[Spencer, Indiana]], after leaving Valparaiso while also studying for a [[Bachelor of Arts]] from [[Indiana University Bloomington|Indiana University]].

He earned two degrees from Indiana: a [[BA degree]] in 1888, and [[Master of Arts]] in 1890. He was the first person to receive a degree in mathematics from Indiana University.<ref>{{cite web |title=Elbert Frank Cox - Evansville Boneyard John Baburnich Living |url=https://web.usi.edu/boneyard/cox.htm |website=web.usi.edu |accessdate=6 February 2020}}</ref> He became a professor of mathematics at [[Vincennes University]] in 1888 until 1891.<ref name=":0" /> He was hired as head of the mathematics department at Indiana in 1891 and continued in that position until 1909. During that period, he did graduate work at [[Stanford University]] and earned a PhD in mathematics from the [[University of Pennsylvania]] in 1897.<ref name="Boop" /><ref name=":0" />

==Maine==
Aley became the 5th President of the [[University of Maine]] in [[Orono, Maine]], in January 1911.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Fernald |first=Merritt Caldwell |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2xC77820qLMC |title=History of the Maine State College and the University of Maine |date=1916 |publisher=University of Maine |pages=159 |language=en |via=[[Google Books]]}}</ref> A fervent supporter of United States involvement in [[World War I]], he made attendance mandatory for pro-war events in and near the campus.<ref>Smith, David C. "The First Century: A History of the University of Maine, 1865-1965." (1979), p. 102.</ref>

On April 19, 1919, during the [[Red Summer]], an incident took place at night at Hannibal Hamlin Hall, University of Maine in which two African American students and brothers Samuel E. Courtney Jr. (1897–1929) and Roger Davis Courtney (1901–1930) were [[tarred and feathered]] by a white mob.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sieber |first=Karen |date=February 7, 2022 |title=In 1919, a Mob in Maine Tarred and Feathered Two Black College Students |url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/in-1919-a-mob-in-maine-tarred-and-feathered-two-black-college-students-180979492/ |access-date=2025-09-11 |website=Smithsonian Magazine |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=May 1, 1919 |title=Near Race Riot Follows Hazing Univ. of Maine |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/evening-express-near-race-riot-follows-h/180852117/ |access-date=2025-09-11 |work=Evening Express |pages=17 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> The event was described by President Aley as a [[hazing]] event and not race related.<ref name=":02">{{Cite news |date=May 3, 1919 |title=Courtney Brothers Hazing Incident |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/kennebec-journal-courtney-brothers-hazin/172717914/ |access-date=2025-09-11 |work=Kennebec Journal |pages=10 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=May 3, 1919 |title=Statement by President Aley |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/commercial-statement-by-president-aley/180852085/ |access-date=2025-09-11 |work=Commercial |pages=3 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> Both of the Courtney brothers transferred to other universities as a result.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sieber |first=Karen |date=February 8, 2021 |title=The hidden story of when two Black college students were tarred and feathered |url=http://theconversation.com/the-hidden-story-of-when-two-black-college-students-were-tarred-and-feathered-147895 |access-date=2025-09-11 |website=[[The Conversation (website)|The Conversation]] |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Death ==
Aley died of pneumonia in 1935 at the age of 72, in his home in New York City.<ref>{{Cite news |date=November 18, 1935 |title=DR. R. J. Aley Dead; University Head; President of Maine From 1910 to 1921, Then of Butler Till Retirement 4 Years Ago. (Published 1935) |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1935/11/18/archives/dr-r-j-jiley-dead-ijnitersities-head-president-of-maine-from-1910.html |access-date=2025-09-11 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en}}</ref>
